title: Should this be the year I finally leave?
summary: Wondering if this should be the year you leave? Why the calendar isn't evidence, and how to tell a chosen year from another postponed one.
body_markdown:
It tends to arrive quietly. You are stacking plates after everyone has gone home, or awake at 2am on an ordinary Tuesday, and you catch yourself thinking a sentence you have thought before. Not a new one. The exact same one, in the same kitchen, with a whole year in between.


If you are asking whether this should be the year you finally leave, you are probably not asking because something happened. You are asking because nothing did.


So, honestly, up front: the calendar cannot answer this, and neither can anyone who has not lived inside your relationship. But the question is a real question. It deserves something better than another twelve months of being put off.


## Why the date is doing so much of the work


New Years, anniversaries, birthdays, the week between Christmas and January: these are audit moments. They are the handful of days a year when you are forced to compare where you are against where you expected to be, and most people do not go looking for that comparison. It shows up whether you want it or not.


That is worth naming, because it cuts two ways.


The date is not evidence that you should leave. Nothing about your relationship changed at midnight. The pull toward a clean slate is strong right now and it will make leaving feel more obvious than it did in August, which is not the same as it being more correct.


But the date is also not a reason to dismiss the question. "I only feel this way because it's January" is one of the more convincing ways people talk themselves out of something they have felt all year. The season did not create the thought. It just took away the place you were hiding it.


## The sentence we hear over and over in Maia conversations


People almost never open with a catastrophe. When someone brings this question to Maia, it usually starts with an apology for how small it sounds. No affair. No shouting. Nothing anyone would call a reason.


What they describe instead is a list of unremarkable things. He is kind. She is a good mother. We do not really fight. And then, somewhere in the middle, almost as an aside, they mention how long it has been.


That aside is the whole thing. They came to ask whether it is bad enough to leave, and the honest answer is that badness was never what they were measuring. Duration was. What has actually accumulated is not a grievance, it is time: the specific, non-refundable experience of watching yourself say the same sentence to yourself for the third January in a row.


People also tend to arrive with the wrong question attached. They ask whether the relationship is broken enough to justify ending it, as if they need to build a case. Most of them never wanted a case. They wanted permission to stop waiting.


## Are you staying for it, or staying from it?


This is the distinction that usually does more work than any list of pros and cons.


Staying *for* the relationship means there is something in it you actively want another year of. Not a memory of it, not a version you are hoping returns. Something present tense.


Staying *from* the alternative means the relationship is not what is holding you. The cost of leaving is: the money, the kids, your parents, the apartment, the terror of being on your own at forty-three. Those are real, heavy, legitimate things, and[fear of what comes after](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/i-want-to-leave-but-im-scared) keeps a lot of people in place for years without ever quite admitting that is what is happening.


Neither answer decides anything for you. Plenty of people look at that honestly, see that they are staying from rather than for, and choose to stay anyway because the cost is genuinely too high right now. That is a defensible choice. It is a very different life from one where you have never let yourself notice.


## One more year is a real answer. Drifting into one is not.


There is a version of "not this year" that is an actual decision, and a version that is just the absence of one. They look identical from the outside and they feel completely different from the inside twelve months later.


The difference is whether anything is specified. "We'll work on it" is not a plan, it is the feeling of having made one. If last January's promise never turned into a behavior with a shape, that is not proof that your partner was lying to you. It is usually proof that nothing concrete was ever on the table, which is also how[a genuine apology can repeat itself for years without changing anything](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/my-partner-apologizes-but-nothing-changes) .


So if you land on another year, give it edges:


- **Name one thing, not the whole relationship.** Not "we need to reconnect." Something you could film. We go to bed at the same time. You tell me when you are upset instead of going quiet for two days.
- **Say what you will do differently, out loud, first.** A year that only requires your partner to change is not a year of work, it is a year of waiting with extra steps.
- **Decide now what "it changed" would look like.** Write it down somewhere you will find it. Future you will be very good at grading generously.
- **Pick a real date to look at it again.** Not next New Year by default. Three months is long enough to see movement and short enough that you have not spent another year finding out.
- **Say the deadline out loud, or admit you have not.** A private ultimatum your partner does not know about is not a chance you gave them.


If you do that and nothing shifts, you will not be back here next January asking the same question with no new information. You will have some. That is the entire point.


## A note on timing, since it is probably on your mind


Some people reading this are not really weighing whether, they are weighing when. That is its own question and it has its own traps, most of them about[not wanting to be the person who ruined a specific date on the calendar](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/break-up-before-the-holidays-or-wait) . If that is closer to where you are, the honest work is different: not whether the relationship is fixable, but what you are buying with the delay and who it is actually for.


And if you genuinely do not know yet whether this is a bad stretch or the end of something, that is a separate question too, and a fair one. It is worth sitting with[whether the problem is repairable](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/should-i-break-up-or-keep-trying) before you spend a year on either answer.


## Before you decide anything


You do not have to resolve this tonight. Almost nobody decides something this size in one sitting, and the people who try usually end up deciding twice.


What helps first is getting the question clean. Most people are carrying three or four questions stacked on top of each other (is this fixable, do I still love them, could I survive leaving, am I allowed to want more) and trying to answer all of them at once, which is why it never resolves.


If you want to pull yours apart, Maia is built for exactly this: a private conversation where you can say the unsayable version out loud, get asked the questions nobody in your life is neutral enough to ask, and find out what you actually think before you tell anyone else. Not to talk you into leaving, and not to talk you into staying. Just to stop you spending another year unsure which one you are doing.
